[Abstract] Large Language Models (LLMs) showcase impressive capabilities but encounter challenges like hallucination, outdated knowledge, and non-transparent, untraceable reasoning processes. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a promising solution by incorporating knowledge from external databases. This enhances the accuracy and credibility of the generation, particularly for knowledge-intensive tasks, and allows for continuous knowledge updates and integration of domain-specific information. RAG synergistically merges LLMs’ intrinsic knowledge with the vast, dynamic repositories of external databases. This comprehensive review paper offers a detailed examination of the progression of RAG paradigms, encompassing the Naive RAG, the Advanced RAG, and the Modular RAG. It meticulously scrutinizes the tripartite foundation of RAG frameworks, which includes the retrieval, the generation and the augmentation techniques. The paper highlights the state-of-the-art technologies embedded in each of these critical components, providing a profound understanding of the advancements in RAG systems. Furthermore, this paper introduces up-to-date evaluation framework and benchmark. At the end, this article delineates the challenges currently faced and points out prospective avenues for research and development 111Resources are available at https://github.com/Tongji-KGLLM/RAG-Survey .

papers.full_text_excerpt:
[Abstract.] In customer service technical support, swiftly and accurately retrieving relevant past issues is critical for efficiently resolving customer inquiries. The conventional retrieval methods in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for large language models (LLMs) treat a large corpus of past issue tracking tickets as plain text, ignoring the crucial intra-issue structure and inter-issue relations, which limits performance. We introduce a novel customer service question-answering method that amalgamates RAG with a knowledge graph (KG). Our method constructs a KG from historical issues for use in retrieval, retaining the intra-issue structure and inter-issue relations. During the question-answering phase, our method parses consumer queries and retrieves related sub-graphs from the KG to generate answers. This integration of a KG not only improves retrieval accuracy by preserving customer service structure information but also enhances answering quality by mitigating the effects of text segmentation. Empirical assessments on our benchmark datasets, utilizing key retrieval (MRR, Recall@K, NDCG@K) and text generation (BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR) metrics, reveal that our method outperforms the baseline by 77.6% in MRR and by 0.32 in BLEU. Our method has been deployed within LinkedIn’s customer service team for approximately six months and has reduced the median per-issue resolution time by 28.6%.

[6. Conclusions and Future Work] In conclusion, our research significantly advances automated question answering systems for customer service. Integrating retrieval augmented generation (RAG) with a knowledge graph (KG) has improved retrieval and answering metrics, and overall service effectiveness. Future work will focus on: developing an automated mechanism for extracting graph templates, enhancing system adaptability; investigating dynamic updates to the knowledge graph based on user queries to improve real-time responsiveness; and exploring the system’s applicability in other contexts beyond customer service.

[3. Methods] We introduce an LLM-based customer service question answering system that seamlessly integrates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with a knowledge graph (KG). Our system (Figure 1) comprises two phases: First, during the KG construction phase, our system constructs a comprehensive knowledge graph from historical customer service issue tickets. It integrates a tree-structured representation of each issue and interlinks them based on relational context. It also generates embedding for each node to facilitate later semantic searching. Second, during the question-answering phase, our method parses consumer queries to identify named entities and intents. It then navigates within the KG to identify related sub-graphs for generating answers.

report_markdown:
## Overview
Retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) promises to ground large language models in external knowledge, but its retrieval quality hinges on how documents are split into chunks [6,7]. The user proposes exploiting document structure to build hierarchical chunks before retrieval, an idea that, while conceptually present in the literature, lacks systematic empirical validation.

## Landscape
RAG surveys broadly categorise indexing strategies, including structural indexes that preserve parent‑child relationships and store data summaries at each node [6,7]. Domain‑specific works increasingly recognise the importance of structure: customer‑service systems ignore intra‑issue structure and inter‑issue relations when treating tickets as plain text [16]; financial applications struggle with complex document formats despite vector‑ or KG‑based retrieval [17,25]; and healthcare RAG reviews note that optimal chunking configurations remain under‑investigated [11,15,22]. Recent papers propose multi‑granular chunking for electronic health records [23] and compare basic chunking methods on academic theses [24], but systematic evaluation of structure‑aware, hierarchical chunking is absent. Knowledge graphs have been combined with RAG to maintain structural consistency [2,16,17], yet no controlled benchmarks contrast them with layout‑based hierarchical chunking.

## Research gaps
- **Structure‑based vs. graph‑based indexing** – No work systematically compares hierarchical, structure‑aware chunking against knowledge‑graph‑based retrieval for knowledge‑intensive tasks [6,16,17]. While [6] describes structural indexes with parent‑child links, and [16] uses KGs to preserve intra‑issue structure, a direct benchmark is missing.
- **Impact of structure‑aware chunking** – The effect of exploiting headings, sections, tables, or other document hierarchy on retrieval quality is largely unexplored. Existing evaluations test only fixed‑size, recursive, or semantic clustering on flat text [24]; the crucial structure ignored in [16] is never systematically varied or measured.
- **Preservation of internal document structure** – RAG surveys and best‑practice studies [6,19] do not address how section‑ and subsection‑level relations should be preserved, split, or represented during chunking to optimise generation quality [6,16,24].
- **Hallucination reduction in domain‑specific RAG** – No empirical study isolates the effect of hierarchical chunking on faithfulness or evidence attribution in healthcare, legal, or financial settings. Current medical RAG evaluations focus on answering accuracy, not on how chunking influences factual errors [9,11,13,15,22,25].
- **Multi‑granular chunking for longitudinal data** – EHR‑RAGp proposes event‑based, time‑based, visit‑level, and care‑stage chunking strategies for electronic health records but explicitly leaves their comparative evaluation as future work [23].

## Novelty
**Score: 40/100**  
The concept of building hierarchical chunks from document structure overlaps directly with the “Structural Index” described in the RAG survey [6], which discusses parent‑child chunk relationships and node‑level summaries. While the identified gaps confirm that rigorous empirical comparison of such chunking is lacking, the core idea is not new. A well‑designed implementation and evaluation could add a meaningful angle, but the proposal as stated does not go beyond existing conceptual descriptions.

open_gaps: There is a lack of systematic comparison between structure-based chunking (exploiting document layout) and knowledge-graph-based indexing for enhancing RAG in knowledge-intensive domains. Existing approaches either use vector representations over raw text chunks or construct separate knowledge graphs, but do not benchmark hierarchical, structure-aware chunking against graph-based retrieval under controlled settings.

Existing RAG surveys and best-practice studies do not address how the internal structure of source documents (sections, subsections, tables, hierarchical relations) should be preserved, split, or represented during the chunking and retrieval phase to optimize generation quality.

The effect of hierarchical chunking on faithfulness and hallucination reduction in domain-specific RAG (e.g., healthcare, legal, financial) is not empirically measured against simpler chunking baselines. Current medical and legal RAG evaluations focus on answering accuracy but neglect how structure-aware chunking might improve evidence attribution or reduce factual errors.
